readerTitle: How you close is the last thing people remember
caseNote: 실제 기업 사례 (Google Stadia 종료, 2022~2023) + 가상 적용 (사내 제품팀, 식당 폐업)
insight: 폐업은 사업의 마지막 제품이다. 고객, 직원, 거래처에 진 빚을 먼저 갚도록 돈과 시간을 남겨 두고, 일찍 정직하게 알릴 때 신뢰가 다음 일로 이어진다.
misconception: 문을 닫기로 했다면 마지막 날까지 조용히 영업해 한 푼이라도 더 버는 것이 낫다. 망한 사업의 마무리 방식은 중요하지 않다.

sources.text: Google, The Keyword blog: Phil Harrison, "A message about Stadia and our long term streaming strategy" (29 September 2022)
Google Stadia Help Center: refund and shutdown FAQ (2022~2023)
Stadia controller Bluetooth mode announcement (December 2022 / January 2023)

factChecks.note: Stadia 종료 발표일 2022년 9월 29일, 서비스 종료일 2023년 1월 18일. 게시 전 Google 공식 블로그로 다시 확인하세요.
환불 범위: Google Store에서 산 Stadia 하드웨어, Stadia 스토어에서 산 게임과 추가 콘텐츠. 발표 직후 신규 구매가 중단되었는지 Help Center로 확인하세요. 카드에는 'stopped taking new purchases'로 적었습니다.
컨트롤러를 다른 기기에서 쓸 수 있게 하는 Bluetooth 전환 도구 제공 시점(2023년 1월 공개)을 확인하세요. 카드에는 연도 없이 'later'로만 적었습니다.
환불 총액, 이용자 수, 직원 처우에 관한 수치는 확인되지 않아 쓰지 않았습니다. 폐업 관련 법적 의무(통지 기간, 상품권, 임금)는 나라마다 다르므로 일반론으로만 다룹니다.

cards.title: How you close is the last thing people remember
body: In 2022, Google decided to close Stadia, the cloud gaming service it had launched three years earlier.
Players had paid for controllers and games that would soon stop working. A failed product usually ends with angry customers. This one ended with many of them saying thank you.

image.label: A game controller on a table with a closing sign
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 거실 탁자 위에 게임 컨트롤러 하나, 옆에 작은 'Closing' 팻말. 따뜻한 조명으로 슬프지만 정돈된 분위기. 실제 Stadia·Google 로고와 제품 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your product is being shut down.
body: You lead a product team inside a large company. Leadership has decided to end your paid service in four months. Customers have bought devices and content from you.
How do you handle the next four months?

options.text: Keep selling, and announce the closure one month before
options.feedback: You earn a little more revenue. But anyone who bought in those three months feels tricked, and the parent company's other products inherit the anger.

options.text: Announce now, stop new sales and refund what customers bought
options.feedback: It costs real money today. In return, customers leave trusting the company enough to buy its next product.

options.text: Announce now, stop new sales, and offer a discount on another product instead of refunds
options.feedback: The honest timing helps. But a voucher asks people who just lost money to trust you again before you've earned it.

cards.title: Google announced early and gave the money back.
body: Google announced the closure on 29 September 2022, almost four months before the service ended on 18 January 2023. It stopped taking new purchases.

Then it **refunded** the controllers bought from its store and the games and add-ons bought on Stadia. Later it released a tool so the controllers could work with other devices instead of becoming junk.
Stadia still failed. But its customers got clear dates, their money back and hardware they could keep using.

cards.title: Shutting down well
body: **Shutting down well** means closing on purpose: telling people early and honestly, and settling what you owe before the money runs out.
The goal changes at the end. You're no longer trying to grow. You're trying to leave the people who trusted you no worse off than necessary.

image.label: A checklist of people to settle with before closing
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 문이 반쯤 닫힌 가게 그림 옆에 체크리스트 네 줄: 'Customers', 'Staff', 'Suppliers', 'Lessons'. 앞의 세 줄은 체크 표시, 마지막 줄은 연필로 쓰는 중.

cards.title: Settle with everyone who trusted you.
body: A good shutdown works through four groups, and it reserves cash for them first.
list: **Customers:** clear dates, refunds for anything unused, a way to keep what they paid for
**Staff:** the truth early, time to find work, help with references
**Suppliers and lenders:** pay what you owe, or agree a plan face to face
**The record:** write down what you learned while it's fresh
cards.callout: Silence feels kinder. It usually just moves the damage to the last day.
cards.softwareNote: In software, what you owe includes customers' data. Give them a simple export and enough time to move to another tool before you switch off.

cards.title: The business ends. The reputation doesn't.
body: Customers, staff and suppliers will judge you by the last chapter, because it's the one they remember.

For a founder, those people are the next venture's first hires, lenders and customers. For a team inside a company, how you close shapes whether leadership trusts you with the next project. A clean ending is how a failure stays a setback instead of becoming a stain.

cards.title: Closing well costs money and needs a plan.
body: Refunds, notice and final wages need cash. If you keep going until the account is empty, you can no longer choose how to close. Deciding earlier leaves room to close well.
Early notice has costs too. Some staff will leave sooner, so some businesses offer a bonus to people who stay to the end.
Rules on notice, wages and gift cards differ by country. Check what applies to you.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant.
body: Your lease ends in six weeks and you won't renew. You have 12 staff, gift cards in customers' wallets, and deposits from two families for parties next month.

options.text: Tell no one until the final week, so staff don't quit early
options.feedback: The schedule stays full. But staff learn they couldn't trust you, and gift-card holders and party hosts find a locked door.

options.text: Tell staff now, stop selling gift cards, honor or refund cards and deposits, and help staff find jobs
options.feedback: You may lose a few shifts and some cash. You keep your name clean with everyone you might need again.

options.text: Tell everyone two weeks before, and honor gift cards only until closing day
options.feedback: Honest, but two weeks is short for staff to find work, and cardholders who miss the window lose their money.

cards.title: Close the way you'd want to be treated.
body: Tell people early, settle what you owe before the money runs out, and keep what you learned.
**Try it today:** list everyone who would lose money or work if your business closed tomorrow. Next to each name, write what you'd owe them.
